Moon Phases

The Moon does not make its own light. What we see as moonlight is sunlight that reflects off the lunar surface back toward Earth.

Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun, just as half of Earth is always in daytime. The phases we see depend on how much of that sunlit half faces us.

As the Moon orbits Earth about once every 29.5 days, the angle between the Sun, Earth and Moon changes, and so does the shape of the lit part we can see.

At new moon, the Moon sits roughly between Earth and the Sun, so the sunlit side faces away from us and the Moon is nearly invisible in the sky.

A few days later a thin waxing crescent appears in the western sky after sunset. Each night the lit part grows as the Moon moves farther along its orbit.

At first quarter we see half of the Moon's disk lit. The terminator, the line between day and night on the Moon, runs straight down the middle of the disk.

Waxing gibbous follows, and then full moon, when Earth sits roughly between the Sun and the Moon and we see the entire sunlit hemisphere facing us.

After full moon the sequence runs in reverse: waning gibbous, third quarter and waning crescent, until the cycle returns to new moon again.

The Moon's shape never actually changes. Only our viewing angle on its sunlit half changes, which is why the phases repeat in the same order every month.

Earth's shadow plays no part in the ordinary phases. It only falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse, which can happen only at full moon.

People in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres see the same phase on the same night, but the lit side appears flipped, because observers in the south see the Moon upside down compared with observers in the north.

The Moon also shows us nearly the same face all the time, because it rotates once on its axis in the same time it takes to orbit Earth. This is called synchronous rotation, and it is why the far side was first photographed only from spacecraft.
